extracted.intended_audience: agency officials, stakeholders considering or participating in negotiated rulemaking, public commenters, and administrative law practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on using negotiated rulemaking (reg-neg) for drafting proposed regulations, including statutory notice and participation requirements, FACA connections, committee composition, and the practical implications for submitting comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of negotiated rulemaking (core concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: In certain situations it is possible to bring together representatives of an agency and the various affected interest groups to negotiate the text of a proposed rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negotiated rulemaking (also called 'regulatory negotiation' or 'reg-neg') is an alternative to traditional rule-drafting procedures; it is appropriate when stakeholders can be convened to negotiate text collaboratively. The page notes the process emerged in the 1980s and is an alternative approach to drafting proposed regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public notice of planned negotiated rulemaking proceedings (Section 564)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 564 requires public notice of planned negotiated rulemaking proceedings both in the Federal Register and in appropriate trade and specialized publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must publish notice of planned reg-neg proceedings in the Federal Register and in appropriate trade/specialized outlets so potentially affected parties are informed. This is a statutory requirement under the Negotiated Rulemaking Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity for persons who believe they are not adequately represented to apply for committee membership
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons or interests believing that they are not adequately represented on the negotiating committee must be given an opportunity to apply for membership, though the agency retains discretion as to whether to grant such requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must provide an application opportunity to allegedly underrepresented parties; however, the agency has discretion to accept or deny membership requests. This balances inclusion with agency control over committee composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory findings regarding need for a negotiated rulemaking committee (FACA connection)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Negotiated Rulemaking Act provides some of the same protections as FACA, requiring that the agency make certain findings regarding the need for a negotiated rulemaking committee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before convening a committee, agencies must make required findings (consistent with FACA-related protections) that justify using negotiated rulemaking—i.e., show that the procedure is needed or appropriate for the issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee balance requirement (representative composition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure committees are balanced to include representatives from all relevant stakeholder communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committees should be constructed to reflect representation across affected interests so that the negotiating body is not biased toward a single viewpoint. Balance is a statutory/administrative concern tied to FACA protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notices and openness of meetings governed by FACA
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirements pertaining to notices and openness of meetings stem from FACA rather than from the Negotiated Rulemaking Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must follow FACA rules about meeting notices and openness when conducting negotiated rulemaking committees, including applicable public-access and transparency obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of comments: committee participation is most influential
rubrics_metrics.description: In a reg-neg context: Comments are most influential if submitted as part of negotiating committee participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participating on the negotiating committee gives stakeholders the greatest ability to shape proposed text. This indicates that engagement via committee membership is more impactful than submission-only strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to submit outside comments on the resulting NPRM
rubrics_metrics.description: Outside commenters can still submit on the resulting NPRM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a negotiated-rule text is produced, the normal notice-and-comment process still applies: those not on the committee retain the statutory right to comment on the notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM).

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee balance disputes as grounds for separate participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Committee balance disputes provide grounds for separate participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an interest believes the committee is unbalanced or inadequately representative, that dispute can be a basis for requesting separate participation or otherwise contesting the process; this is a procedural lever for excluded stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference to reg-neg-derived proposals and higher burden for comment challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Reg-neg-derived proposals receive deference - challenges via comment must be especially well-grounded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals stemming from negotiated rulemaking may receive deference because they reflect negotiated agreement; therefore, comments that seek to overturn or significantly alter such proposals should present particularly strong, well-grounded arguments and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow ACUS recommendations (notably Recommendation 2017-2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The negotiated rulemaking process was developed primarily in the 1980s and fleshed out in recommendations by the Administrative Conference of the United States (ACUS), including Recommendation 2017-2 on Negotiated Rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies and participants should consult ACUS recommendations (e.g., Recommendation 2017-2) for best practices and further detail on conducting and structuring negotiated rulemaking effectively.
